title: A new earth (Isaiah 65:17–25)
hookLine: a vision of no weeping, houses built and lived in, the wolf and lamb at peace
carry: nobody's harvest goes to someone else
tomorrow: Say not, I am a child (Jeremiah 1:4–10)
last: THE LIGHT CAME BEFORE YOU DID.

lines: A HOUSE, BUILT AND LIVED IN.
cards: A house with someone living in it who also built it. A vineyard where the person who planted the vines gets to drink the wine. A baby who grows up.
An old man who lives out all his days. Children who stay with their parents. That's the list.
Near the end of Isaiah, the prophet describes a whole new creation, and it turns out to look like an ordinary street on a good afternoon. No golden throne room, no clouds.
Just the plain, unbroken things that war and exile kept taking away.

teach.h: NEW HEAVENS AND A NEW EARTH.
teach.b: It opens big: "For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind." Then, almost at once, it comes down to street level.

teach.h: NO MORE THE VOICE OF WEEPING.
teach.b: Jerusalem will be a joy, and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying.
And the heart of it: "And they shall build houses, and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them."

teach.h: THEY SHALL NOT HURT NOR DESTROY.
teach.b: The next verse says it the other way around: they shall not build, and another inhabit; they shall not plant, and another eat.
For a people who had watched their houses taken and their fields stripped, that is what a new earth means. Not escape from the world. The world, with the theft taken out of it.
Your work stays yours. Your children grow up.
Then the vision reaches back to an earlier picture in Isaiah, the one from ten days ago: the wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock.
And it ends: they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain. The long walk through Isaiah closes on a promise made of ordinary things.
Some Jews speak of tikkun olam, repairing the world, as part of the work of moving toward a vision like this one. Different communities hold different hopes for how and when it comes.
The text itself keeps it plain: a house, a vine, a long life, and no one hurting anyone on the mountain.

how: Jews read Isaiah's visions of a repaired world as part of the prophets, and some connect them with tikkun olam, the work of repairing the world through justice and kindness.

o: repairing the world, bit by bit
a blessing said over a newly built house
a year when the fields rest from work

games.q: a new earth — tap the pairs.
p: and eat the fruit of them

s: Isaiah's new earth is a world of clouds and thrones
it's houses lived in, vineyards enjoyed, children who grow up.
in the vision, no one builds a house for someone else to live in
they shall not build, and another inhabit.
the wolf and the lamb appear only once in Isaiah
chapter 11 has the wolf and the lamb, and chapter 65 brings them back.

games.q: you're a prophet describing a brand-new creation to people who lost their homes. what do you put at the center?
o: a palace of gold in the sky.
people living in the houses they built.
a world with no work at all.
games.why: "they shall build houses, and inhabit them." the new earth is the old one with the theft taken out.

practice: Choose one small place you know well, your street, a school, a hospital ward, a park, and let it be mended in your mind. Who lives there safely, who gets to keep what they built, who stops crying?
See it in plain detail, and if you pray, you can hold the verse: they shall not hurt nor destroy.

wordCard.voice: Tikkun olam. Repairing the world, the work some Jews do toward Isaiah's vision of a new earth: houses built and lived in, vineyards planted and enjoyed. Today's word.
